articles.full_text:
Vanguard Finds Younger Investors Choose ESG Voting at Twice Older Rate
- Younger investors showed the strongest preference for ESG-focused proxy voting, with 38.8% of investors under 30 selecting the Glass Lewis ESG Policy, versus 16.2% of investors aged 62 to 80.
- Investor Choice participation increased more than sixfold, rising from 82,000 investors in 2025 to 507,000 in 2026. Participating assets climbed from $9 billion to $151 billion.
- Vanguard plans to extend Investor Choice to all U.S. equity index funds in 2027, potentially increasing eligible assets from about $4 trillion to $8 trillion.
Vanguard’s latest proxy voting data has revealed a sharp generational divide in how investors approach ESG and corporate governance, as participation in its Investor Choice program reached more than half a million investors in 2026.
The investment manager’s How Investors Vote report found that younger investors selected its ESG-focused voting policy at more than twice the rate of the oldest age group surveyed. Female investors were also considerably more likely than male investors to choose the ESG option.
The findings come as Vanguard rapidly expands Investor Choice, which allows eligible fund investors to select the proxy voting policy applied to their proportionate holdings.
Younger investors lean toward ESG voting
The Glass Lewis ESG Policy was the most popular option among Vanguard investors under 46 participating in the program.
Among investors under 30, 38.8% selected the policy. The figure was 36.3% for investors aged 31 to 45.
That compared with 19.4% among investors aged 46 to 61 and 16.2% for those aged 62 to 80.
The policy follows Glass Lewis recommendations based on the view that investment returns can benefit from identifying, disclosing and mitigating ESG-related risks.
Younger investors also showed a different preference from older participants in their broader governance choices. Vanguard found that older investors were more likely to select its Company Board-Aligned Policy, which votes according to recommendations made by portfolio company boards.
Gender differences were also pronounced. Female investors selected the Glass Lewis ESG Policy at a rate of 25%, compared with 15% among male investors.
The findings offer asset managers a clearer picture of how investor preferences around governance and ESG can differ substantially across demographic groups.
Investor Choice participation surges
Investor Choice has grown considerably since Vanguard launched the program in 2023.
The number of participating investors increased from 82,000 in 2025 to 507,000 in 2026. Participating assets rose nearly 17-fold, from $9 billion to $151 billion.
Nearly 80 retirement plan sponsors now participate, representing more than one million underlying plan participants.
RELATED ARTICLE: Vanguard to Introduce Environmental Opportunities Fund
Eligible assets also expanded from around $1 trillion to approximately $4 trillion in 2026. Vanguard plans another major expansion next year. All of its U.S. equity index funds are expected to become eligible in 2027, bringing the potential asset pool to approximately $8 trillion.
Investors have already selected policies for another $120 billion of assets held in funds expected to join the program next year.
“Investor Choice is grounded in the foundational belief that investors have diverse perspectives on corporate governance, and those perspectives deserve to be heard. More than half a million investors have chosen to participate in Investor Choice this year, demonstrating strong demand and reinforcing the importance of giving index fund investors a voice.” John Galloway, Global Head of Investor Engagement at Vanguard, said “Vanguard expects the expansion to give more investors direct influence over how their funds vote.”
ESG share shifts as the program expands
Despite its popularity among younger participants, the Glass Lewis ESG Policy’s overall asset-weighted share fell from 18% to 12% in 2026.
Vanguard attributed the change largely to the expansion of Investor Choice and the resulting shift in the mix of participating shareholders.
Its ESG U.S. Stock ETF provides a contrasting picture. Among investors in that fund, selection of the ESG policy increased from 73% in 2023 to 78% in 2026, despite investors having more policy choices available.
Across the broader program, no single voting policy accounted for more than 38% of selections.
For asset managers, boards and governance teams, the data highlights an increasingly fragmented proxy voting landscape. As investor choice programs scale, stewardship policies may need to accommodate wider differences in shareholder preferences rather than relying on a single institutional voting approach.
Vanguard’s planned expansion to $8 trillion of eligible assets could make those differences more consequential. It will also provide a larger test of whether demographic gaps in ESG voting preferences persist as investor-directed proxy voting moves further into mainstream index investing.

articles.full_text:
Veolia

According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Post Consumer Recycled Plastics market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global Post Consumer Recycled Plastics market is entering a phase of structural expansion, transitioning from a voluntary sustainability initiative to a compliance-driven industry. Regulatory mandates, particularly in Europe and parts of Asia-Pacific, are setting minimum recycled content thresholds for packaging, while major consumer brands have committed to significant PCR incorporation by 2030 and beyond. This report analyzes the market from 2026 to 2035, covering key polymer types such as PET, HDPE, PP, LDPE, PVC, PS, and engineering plastics.
The value chain spans collection, sorting, processing, pelletizing, and compounding, with demand concentrated in packaging, building and construction, automotive, consumer goods, and textiles. Supply-side constraints, including inconsistent collection infrastructure and quality standardization challenges, remain critical. The forecast period is expected to witness technological maturation, supply chain consolidation, and deeper integration of PCR into product design. The analysis provides a data-driven view for manufacturers, investors, and advisors navigating this evolving landscape.
The baseline scenario for the Post Consumer Recycled Plastics market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates robust growth, underpinned by regulatory push and corporate pull. Packaging remains the dominant end-use sector, driven by recycled content mandates in the EU and increasing voluntary commitments from global brands. The market is expected to grow at a CAGR of 7.2%, reaching a market index of 200 by 2035 (2025=100). This growth is supported by expanding collection and sorting infrastructure, particularly in Asia-Pacific and Europe, and advancements in mechanical recycling technologies that improve quality and yield.
However, the market faces headwinds from volatile virgin plastic prices, which can undermine the cost competitiveness of PCR, and from limited availability of high-quality feedstock. The supply chain is gradually consolidating, with waste management firms and specialized recyclers investing in capacity. North America and Europe will remain key markets, while Asia-Pacific emerges as both a major producer and consumer. The forecast assumes no major regulatory rollbacks and continued brand commitments, leading to a steady increase in PCR penetration across durable and non-durable goods.
Packaging is the largest and most dynamic end-use sector for post-consumer recycled plastics, accounting for nearly half of global demand. The sector's growth is propelled by recycled content mandates, such as the EU's Single-Use Plastics Directive and similar measures in Asia-Pacific, which require minimum PCR incorporation in beverage bottles and other packaging. Major brands like Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, and Unilever have pledged to use significant recycled content by 2030, creating a steady demand pull. Mechanically recycled PET (rPET) and HDPE are the primary materials, with rPET demand outstripping supply in many regions.
Through 2035, demand-side indicators such as recycled content targets, EPR fees, and consumer labeling requirements will be critical. The sector will also see increased use of recycled PP and LDPE in flexible packaging, though technical challenges remain. The shift toward mono-material packaging and design for recycling will further boost PCR uptake. Current trend: Increasing regulatory mandates and brand commitments drive strong demand for recycled PET and HDPE in beverage bottles, food containers, and flexible packaging..
Major trends: Rising recycled content mandates for beverage bottles and food-contact packaging, Brand commitments to achieve 25-50% recycled content by 2030, Advancements in sorting and decontamination technologies enabling food-grade rPET, Growth in flexible packaging recycling, though still limited by technical hurdles, and Increased use of recycled HDPE in non-food packaging and industrial containers.
Representative participants: Amcor plc, Berry Global Group, Inc, Plastipak Holdings, Inc, Indorama Ventures Public Company Limited, and Veolia Environnement S.A.
Building and construction is a significant and growing end-use sector for post-consumer recycled plastics, driven by the need for durable, cost-effective, and sustainable materials. Recycled PVC and HDPE are widely used in pipes, window profiles, flooring, and insulation, where long product lifespans and low maintenance requirements align with circular economy principles. The construction sector's demand is less sensitive to brand-driven sustainability mandates but is increasingly influenced by green building certifications and government procurement policies favoring recycled content. Through 2035, infrastructure spending and renovation activities in both developed and emerging economies will support steady demand.
However, the sector faces competition from virgin materials and alternative materials like wood and concrete. Key demand-side indicators include construction output, green building standards, and the availability of high-quality recycled PVC and HDPE. Technological improvements in sorting and processing will enhance the suitability of PCR for structural applications. Current trend: Durable applications such as pipes, profiles, and insulation benefit from cost advantages and sustainability credentials of recycled PVC and HDPE..
Major trends: Growing adoption of recycled PVC in pipes and profiles due to cost and durability, Green building certifications and government procurement policies promoting recycled content, Infrastructure investment and renovation projects driving demand for recycled HDPE, Development of composite materials combining PCR with other recycled materials, and Challenges in sourcing consistent, high-quality recycled PVC feedstock.
Representative participants: Veolia Environnement S.A, Suez S.A, Waste Management, Inc, Republic Services, Inc, and KW Plastics.
The automotive sector is a rapidly growing end-use market for post-consumer recycled plastics, driven by regulatory pressures and corporate sustainability goals. Recycled PP and engineering plastics are used in interior components, battery housings, and under-the-hood parts, where they offer weight reduction and cost benefits. The EU's End-of-Life Vehicles Directive and similar regulations in other regions are pushing automakers to incorporate recycled content. Major automakers like Volkswagen, Ford, and Toyota have set targets for recycled material use, creating a demand pull.
Through 2035, the shift toward electric vehicles will open new opportunities for PCR in battery casings and interior parts, though technical requirements for flame retardancy and durability remain stringent. Demand-side indicators include vehicle production volumes, recycled content mandates, and the availability of high-quality recycled engineering plastics. The sector's growth will also depend on the development of closed-loop recycling systems for automotive plastics. Current trend: Automakers increasingly use recycled PP and engineering plastics for interior and under-the-hood parts to meet circularity targets and reduce weight..

Representative participants: MBA Polymers, Inc, Veolia Environnement S.A, Suez S.A, Loop Industries, Inc, and Far Eastern New Century Corporation.
Consumer goods represent a diverse and growing end-use sector for post-consumer recycled plastics, encompassing household items, electronics, toys, and durable goods. Demand is largely driven by brand image and consumer preference for sustainable products, as well as corporate commitments to reduce virgin plastic use. Recycled HDPE, PP, and PS are commonly used in these applications, where color and consistency requirements are less stringent than in packaging. Major brands like IKEA, Philips, and Procter & Gamble have incorporated PCR into their products, signaling a broader trend. Through 2035, the sector will benefit from increasing consumer awareness and regulatory measures such as EPR schemes.
Demand-side indicators include retail sales of sustainable products, brand sustainability reports, and consumer sentiment surveys. However, the sector faces challenges related to the availability of food-grade and high-quality recycled plastics, as well as competition from virgin materials. Innovations in recycling and design for recyclability will be key to sustaining growth. articles.title: National authorities must work together to ensure consistent enforcement of EUDR - Oils & Fats International
articles.summary: National authorities must work together to ensure consistent enforcement of EUDR  Oils & Fats International
articles.full_text:
With the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) coming into force from 1 January, national authorities need to be aligned to prevent palm oil entering Europe through more lenient entry points, the OFI Commercial/Technical conference heard in Amsterdam last week.
The conference was one of four held under one roof from 21-23 September at the OFI International 2026 show, which attracted more than 350 people from over 30 countries.
“The EUDR is a welcome and loved baby but its delivery has been long and painful,” said Ruben Brunsveld, deputy director, market transformation EMEA, the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO).
Originally due to take effect on 30 December 2024, the EUDR has been delayed twice but is now set to come into force for large- and medium-sized companies on 1 January, and for small and micro operators on 30 June 2027.
Companies placing palm oil, soya, cocoa, coffee, cattle, rubber or timber goods on the EU market will need to have a functioning due diligence system to prove these commodities are deforestation-free, legally produced and traceable to their source.
Brunsveld told the conference that while RSPO certification did not substitute an operator’s due diligence responsibilities, it could demonstrate compliance in required risk analysis, traceability and National Competent Authority (NCA) checks.
He identified three outstanding issues in the implementation of the EUDR – data sharing, the new Annex 1 to the EUDR, and different national approaches to implementation.
Data sharing: Under the EUDR, companies will need to submit due diligence statements (DDSs) into an EU information system, throwing up questions on who owns the data, who has access to it, and the protection of sensitive commercial information.
Annex 1: The July 2026 revision of Annex I - which determines which products fall within the EUDR - removed some products from scope and added others, including certain palm oil derivatives. The new products would become subject to the EUDR from 30 December 2027, and it remained to be seen how companies would respond to this, Ruben said.
National implementation: While the EUDR is an EU law, it is up to each country’s NCA to enforce it.
Ruben said NCAs needed to be aligned to prevent different entry points into Europe, especially if some NCAs were more lenient in enforcing the EUDR than others.
Marieke Leegwater, senior policy advisor at Solidaridad, added that there was increasing evidence that smallholders were being excluded from EU value chains because of lack of documentation and the complexities of organising data; and it was often unclear how farmer data ownership would be protected.
“For palm oil, smallholders are being pushed out of value chains to Europe. It started with the RSPO and the EUDR has made it worse.”
European palm oil volumes were now mostly supplied from bigger estates and a solution needed to be found to include smallholders, she said.
- EU-Indonesia palm oil trade
Relating to palm oil, Frans Claassen, managing director of MVO – the Netherlands oils and fats industry association – said the new the EU-Indonesia Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) could make Indonesian palm oil significantly more attractive for the EU.
“CEPA will introduce annual duty and levy-free export quotas for Indonesian palm oil to the EU. The quota starts with 1.9M tonnes and increases by 3% for nine consecutive years.”
The agreement – set to come into force in early 2027 – would abolish current 3.8% EU import duties on crude palm oil (CPO); 12.8% duties on solid fractions (immediate packings, maximum 1kg); 10.9% of ‘other’ solid fractions; 5.1% duties on refined/bleach/deodorised (RBD) palm oil or palm olein for non-food applications; and 9% duties for ‘other’ RBD palm oil or palm olein.
Claassen explained that Indonesia accounted for a 10% share of total EU CPO imports of 1.68M tonnes in 2025, and a 51% share of the EU’s total processed palm oil imports of 1.46M tonnes that year, giving it a 29% share of total EU imports of palm oil.
At the Indonesian September 2026 palm oil reference price of US$1,007.51/tonne, CEPA would remove US$268.90/tonne in export duties and levies on CPO, and US$176.75/tonne of export duties and levies on RBD palm oil, which could make Indonesian CPO significantly more attractive for the EU.
However, the actual benefits fully depended on how Indonesia allocated the quotas, and European processors needed clarity on the practical operation and allocation of quotas “without delay”, Claassen said.
Dr Fadhil Hasan, senior economist and head of foreign affairs at the Indonesian Palm Oil Association (GAPKI), said that CEPA was in the process of ratification in Indonesia and would be passed in March.
On policy changes related to palm oil, Dr Hasan said the country’s new state-owned entity - Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia (DSI) – had been set up to improve governance in export activities and export earnings management, and to eliminate the risk of under-invoicing and transfer pricing.
“DSI is not the sole exporter of palm oil and other products.”
The government was also setting up a commodity exchange to make and strengthen palm oil price discovery.
And there was a shift in Indonesia’s mandatory biofuel blending programme to emphasise energy security, rather than as instrument to stabilise palm oil prices.
Dr Hasan added that due to strong El Niño effects this year, palm oil production would fall by 4-5M tonnes in 2027. Domestic consumption would increase by around 2M tonnes next year due to full B50 palm oil-based biodiesel mandatory blending, and exports would therefore decline next year.
Vegetable oil squeeze
Artem Hammerschmidt, head of vegetable oils and biofuels research at Cefetra Analytics, also spoke of a “major vegetable oil squeeze” in the next two years.
He said surging energy prices had strengthened the economic case for biofuels, raising the demand outlook for oils and fats.
In the USA, mandate-driven output requirements would rise by around 3M tonnes in 2026 and another 2M tonnes in 2027, forcing US biodiesel/HVO and SAF producers back into imported oils and fats. Indonesia’s palm oil use for biodiesel, driven by its B50 biodiesel mandate, was also set to lift domestic palm oil use for biodiesel to 16.8M tonnes, curtailing exports.
Hammerschmidt said total oils and fats requirements for FAME, HVO and SAF in 2025 totalled 58.9M tonnes but were forecast to jump by 6-7M tonnes in 2026 and by another 7M tonnes in 2027 to total 72.5M tonnes.
“The challenge is not absorbing one exceptional increase but doing so for two consecutive years.”
With El Niño setting the stage for a major vegetable oil squeeze, global production of oils and fats was expected to fall by 0.3M tonnes in 2026/27, exports could fall by 0.8M tonnes and stocks could plunge by 3.3M tonnes as demand jumped 5.7M tonnes, he said.
Limited global supply of used and waste oils also meant Europe would increasingly rely on rapeseed oil as a biofuel feedstock, with producers having to pay more for used cooking oil (UCO) as suppliers would need to go further afield to find and collect new supplies.
UCO
Because UCO is increasingly used as a raw material for biofuels, the EU was introducing new requirements for UCO imports, explained Steven Danneel, Coordinating Senior Inspector, Animal By-products, Tactical Direction & Expertise Division, Directorate Enforcement, of the Netherlands Food and Consumer Products Safety Authority (NVWA).
- Danneel told the OFI Commercial/Technical conference that UCO could originate from vegetable oils such as soyabean and palm oils, or animal-based sources such as tallow.
Under the new rules, due to come into force on 19 November 2027, UCO containing or consisting of animal-origin material would be considered as Category 3 material under the EU Animal By-products (ABP) regulation.
The imported ABP UCO had to originate from an ABP-approved or registered operator in the third country, which would be an issue, he said.
This was because UCO may be collected from many small sources; authorities in the exporting country would have to oversee the different operators and provide relevant information for EU purposes; and existing UCO supply chains may not be structured for this.
- Danneel added that as it was not always possible to test if UCO came from animal origins, traceability would need to be document-based, rather than from analysis of the product.
- The OFI Commercial/Technical Conference was organised by Oils & Fats International (OFI) and MVO - The Netherlands Oils and Fats Industry association.
- The conference and the OFI International 2026 show, held at the Amsterdam Congress Centre, was supported by the Netherlands Oils, Fats and Oilseeds Trade Association (NOFOTA) and FOSFA International. The event also featured a major exhibition of suppliers to the oils and fats industry and three other conferences organised by the German Society for Fat Science (DGF); Euro Fed Lipid (EFL) and Triact.

articles.summary: Have Your Say on the New dlr County Biodiversity Action Plan 2027-2032  Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council
articles.full_text:
dlr is delighted to announce that public consultation is now open on the new dlr County Biodiversity Action Plan 2027-2032.
In 2019, Ireland declared a Biodiversity Crisis, and biodiversity loss continues to affect habitats, wildlife and ecosystems across the country and around the world. The EU Nature Restoration Law 2024 sets targets to help restore nature, and local authorities, including dlr, have an important role in protecting and improving biodiversity by working with local communities, organisations and partners.
The decline of pollinators such as bees is increasingly visible across the county. At the same time, local communities, groups and individuals are doing great work to support nature and protect wildlife. The new plan is an opportunity to build on this momentum, and residents are encouraged to share their ideas.
The consultation documents available to view are:
- A discussion document on biodiversity in dlr
- The previous dlr Biodiversity Action Plan 2021-2025
Speaking about the consultation, An Cathaoirleach of Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council, Councillor Barry Saul, said:
"I am delighted to see the dlr Biodiversity Action Plan 2027-2032 going to public consultation. Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown is an urban county with a variety of important habitats and wildlife, and this Action Plan is an important step towards safeguarding and celebrating that biodiversity.
I encourage everyone to take a moment to contribute their knowledge and insights, helping us to develop a comprehensive plan for the area's natural heritage."
Public engagement sessions
dlr will hold a series of public engagement sessions during the consultation period:
- Friday 9 October, 10am to 1pm: Dundrum Library, Churchtown Road Upper, Dundrum, D14 VP97
- Tuesday 13 October, 11am to 2pm: Dargan Room, Royal Marine Hotel, Marine Road, Dún Laoghaire, A96 K063
- Thursday 15 October, 6pm to 8.30pm: Dalkey Room, The Graduate, Killiney Shopping Centre, Rochestown Avenue, Dún Laoghaire, A96 KA09
- Monday 19 October, 7.30pm to 8.30pm: Online webinar, with dlr's Biodiversity Officer giving a talk on the highlights of the previous plan and an overview of the new plan. Details are available at www.dlrcoco.ie/dlr-events
You can place written submissions in the collection boxes at each in-person session.

Submissions will be kept confidential, used only for planning and policy purposes, and published in a way that does not identify individuals or organisations.

articles.title: Schneider Electric Partners with Greenly to Decarbonize Value Chain SMEs - ESG Today
articles.summary: Schneider Electric Partners with Greenly to Decarbonize Value Chain SMEs  ESG Today
articles.full_text:
Global energy technology company Schneider Electric and carbon accounting solutions provider Greenly announced a new partnership aimed at expanding Schneider electric’s Decarbonization Champion Program (DCP), its program to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the electrical value chain to measure and reduce emissions and unlock value from sustainability initiatives.
Founded in 2019, Paris-based Greenly provides software aimed at enabling companies to monitor, reduce and report emissions. The company’s solutions enable enterprises to manage decarbonization through granular Scope 3 measurement that extends down to the product level.
The companies said that the partnership comes as businesses across global value chains face growing pressure to provide emissions data and support customers’ sustainability goals, requiring SMEs to measure and reduce their carbon footprints Regulations including the European Union’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and Australia’s Climate-Related Financial Disclosure regime are also increasing transparency requirements across value chains.
Through the new partnership, Schneider said that it will provide a structured decarbonization roadmap through its global network of partner SMEs, combining Greenly’s carbon accounting platform with Schneider’s SE Advisory Services sustainability consulting support.
Alexis Normand, CEO and co-founder of Greenly, said:
“Many SMEs want to act on carbon reduction but lack accessible tools and guidance. By combining software with hands-on support, we aim to make decarbonization both measurable and actionable across supply chains.”
According to the companies, the program provides participating partners with access to Schneider Electric’s Sustainability and Energy Tech School and Greenly’s platform for measuring, visualizing, tracking and reporting Scope 1 and 2 emissions. It also includes SE Advisory Services support through remote audits, strategy workshops and the development of decarbonization roadmaps, as well as access to selected Schneider Electric technologies and financial incentives.
Schneider Electric estimated that the program represents more than $34,000 in annual value for each channel partner.
Bin Lu, Executive Vice President, Power Products, Schneider Electric, said:
“Together with Greenly, we are helping our partners build the capabilities needed to meet evolving market expectations, improve operational efficiency, and accelerate decarbonization.”

articles.title: New Direct Travel sustainability report sets context for lower-carbon crew change travel - Cyprus Shipping News

articles.full_text:
New Direct Travel sustainability report sets context for lower-carbon crew change travel
- Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions baseline established across the combined organisation
- Report highlights marine expertise in addressing travel-related emissions across ocean-dependent industries
- ATPI Halo helps shipping companies measure and address Scope 3 emissions associated with crew change travel
Direct Travel, one of the world’s largest travel management companies, has published its first annual Direct Impact Report since the acquisition of long-term partner ATPI, bringing together its sustainability and social impact activity from across the expanded Direct Travel organisation.
Covering key reporting metrics from the 2025 calendar year, the report establishes an important foundation for measuring future progress as Direct Travel continues to expand its global capabilities across corporate travel, specialty travel, leisure travel and meetings & events. It includes ATPI Marine Travel within the group’s Specialty Travel business, which an extensive portfolio of crew change travel services to the maritime sector.
Helping Clients Measure and Reduce Travel Emissions
Beyond its own climate reporting, Direct Travel continued to support clients in taking greater control of their travel emissions, helping them adopt Thrust Carbon’s emissions measurement platform and gain greater visibility of flight, hotel, rail and car hire emissions data.
Direct Travel has also expanded its partnerships across the aviation ecosystem to improve access to Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), an alternative to conventional jet fuel that can reduce greenhouse gas emissions over its lifecycle. Collaborations include fuel producers CFP Energy and Neste, while Direct Travel has also worked with Delta Air Lines to strengthen client understanding of SAF and how it can be integrated into wider sustainability strategies.
Pippa Ganderton, Director, Sustainable Travel and Events, said: “2025 marked an exciting turning point, with more clients preparing for their first sustainability audits and moving from climate ambition towards meaningful action. Accurate emissions data is the vital first step, helping organizations understand and address the environmental impact of their travel and events programmes while responding to growing investor and stakeholder expectations.
Applying the approach to crew change travel
The Direct Impact Report specifically highlights work by the group’s marine and energy teams to advance climate awareness across ocean-dependent industries, connecting travel-related emissions and marine sustainability with the operational realities facing these sectors.
For shipowners and operators, one practical application is crew change travel. While direct vessel emissions remain shipping’s primary decarbonisation challenge, the flights and other transport required to mobilise and repatriate seafarers form part of a company’s wider Scope 3 footprint.
Through ATPI Halo’s Measure, Reduce, Compensate approach, ATPI Marine Travel enables shipping clients to quantify the CO2e associated with crew change travel and use that insight to identify opportunities for reduction. These can include more direct itineraries and informed supplier choices where vessel schedules, port locations and other operational requirements allow.
Where air travel remains unavoidable, maritime clients can also access SAF through ATPI Halo’s partnership with Neste, providing an in-sector route to reducing aviation-related emissions. For residual emissions, Halo provides access to verified carbon compensation projects, including blue carbon initiatives aligned with the marine environment.
The report also highlights the experience of marine client Van Weelde. Carlo Jansen, CFO of Van Weelde, said: “As a business operating within the marine sector, we recognize the importance of supporting long-term environmental responsibility across our operations and supply chain. Working with ATPI Halo has helped us better understand and address our travel-related emissions through more transparent reporting and practical action.”
Christal Bemont, Chief Executive Officer of Direct Travel, added: “This report marks an important milestone for Direct Travel as we present our first sustainability and social impact report reflecting our expanded family of companies, including ATPI and Creative Group. As Direct Travel continues to integrate ATPI and collaborate across Creative Group, we are accelerating the sharing of expertise, innovation, and responsible business practices across our global business.”
Looking beyond the environmental impact
While climate action is a central theme, the Direct Impact Report also reflects Direct Travel’s wider focus on its people, communities and clients. During 2025, around one in six employees took part in volunteering activities, contributing more than 4,525 hours globally, while 30,684 hours of professional and development-focused training were completed across the organisation. Women held 50% of leadership roles, and Direct Travel reported a 98% client retention rate, reflecting a broader approach to responsible growth that extends beyond environmental impact.

articles.title: EY Launches Framework to Put Financial Value on Sustainability Risks
articles.summary:
EY has launched a new framework designed to put financial numbers behind sustainability risks and opportunities, as companies face growing pressure to justify climate and ESG spending in conventional business […]
The post EY Launches Framework to Put Financial Value on Sustainability Risks appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
EY Launches Framework to Put Financial Value on Sustainability Risks
- Financial exposure: EY’s new Sustainability Value Bridge links climate, nature and broader ESG risks directly to enterprise value, costs and revenue.
- Executive focus: The framework applies familiar financial disciplines to areas including supply chains, regulation, capital costs, operations and brand value.
- Investment case: EY aims to give executives and investors a clearer way to assess which sustainability investments protect existing value and which can generate new growth.
EY has launched a new framework designed to put financial numbers behind sustainability risks and opportunities, as companies face growing pressure to justify climate and ESG spending in conventional business terms.
The EY Sustainability Value Bridge seeks to connect sustainability factors directly with financial performance. It focuses on how environmental and social pressures can erode enterprise value, as well as how companies can protect or create value through targeted investment.
The launch comes as sustainability competes with other priorities on some C-suite agendas. At the same time, EY argues that climate, nature and other sustainability-related disruptions are increasingly entering the time horizons used for corporate planning.
In a white paper accompanying the framework, EY said:
“These issues are no longer distant concerns, and the impacts often hide in plain sight because the link to sustainability is often not fully understood, much less quantified. Many companies today are struggling to connect the interrelated, systemic impacts of nature-based and other sustainability-linked changes on their value chains.”
Turning sustainability exposure into financial metrics
At the centre of the framework is a relatively familiar corporate finance concept: a value bridge.
EY divides the financial effects of sustainability into value erosion and value realization. The latter has two components. Value protection focuses on mitigating costs, while value creation examines opportunities to generate new revenue and growth.
Companies first identify sustainability-related costs that could reduce enterprise value. They can then assess actions that protect against those losses before examining opportunities to create incremental value.
Potential erosion factors identified by EY include raw material volatility, supply chain disruption and operational risk. Higher costs of capital and regulatory compliance also feature. Other exposures include reputational damage and volatility involving consumers, employees and communities.
The framework pairs these risks with potential financial levers. These include operational efficiency, supply chain resilience, capital optimization and regulatory proficiency. Brand premiums, product innovation and new business models can provide additional sources of value.
The approach could help finance and sustainability teams develop a common language at a time when investment decisions face greater scrutiny.
Bringing ESG into established financial disciplines
Mark Weick, former Director of Sustainability Programs at Dow, highlighted the framework’s use of financial methods already familiar to executives and investors.
He wrote on LinkedIn:
“This practical new EY Sustainability Value Bridge framework will be very helpful in valuing and prioritizing investments in areas previously thought to be difficult to evaluate.”
Weick also pointed to Dow’s experience developing its 2025 Sustainability Goals. He recalled that then-CFO Howard Ungerleider required a nine-month process to establish a financial rationale for every proposed sustainability goal before the plan went to the board.
RELATED ARTICLE: EY Launches Sustainable Operating Blueprint to Embed ESG Into Core Business Strategy
According to Weick, Dow subsequently reported at least $1 billion in value realized from those goals.
His example highlights a broader governance question facing corporate sustainability teams. Environmental and social initiatives increasingly need to compete for capital alongside conventional investments, with boards expecting measurable financial rationale.
What executives and investors should take away
For C-suite leaders, EY’s framework offers a way to move sustainability discussions closer to capital allocation, risk management and strategic planning. That could become increasingly important as physical climate impacts, supply chain pressures and regulation affect near-term financial assumptions.
Investors may also benefit from more explicit links between sustainability initiatives and enterprise value. A consistent financial framework could make it easier to assess whether spending is primarily defensive, aimed at protecting existing value, or designed to create new revenue.
The approach does not remove the difficulty of quantifying environmental and social impacts. Assumptions around future regulation, climate exposure, consumer behaviour and nature-related dependencies can remain uncertain. However, incorporating those factors into established financial processes can make those assumptions more visible to boards and investors.
EY said:
“Ultimately, sustainability is no longer only about responsibility. It is about protecting value, creating value and securing the viability of the enterprise.”
That shift is becoming central to the global ESG debate. As sustainability budgets face closer scrutiny, the ability to translate environmental and social exposure into financial consequences may increasingly determine which projects receive capital and board-level attention.

articles.title: UK Regulator Drops Mandatory Climate Disclosure Plan for Listed Companies
articles.summary:
Britain’s financial regulator has stepped back from tougher mandatory climate disclosure requirements for listed companies, citing concerns over costs, proportionality and international competitiveness. The Financial Conduct Authority had proposed in […]
The post UK Regulator Drops Mandatory Climate Disclosure Plan for Listed Companies appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
UK Regulator Drops Mandatory Climate Disclosure Plan for Listed Companies
- The Financial Conduct Authority has abandoned plans to make the UK’s new climate reporting standard mandatory for listed companies, retaining its existing “comply or explain” model.
- The decision follows concerns over compliance costs and the UK’s competitiveness as a listing venue, as the EU and US also pull back from stricter climate-reporting requirements.
- Climate disclosure is already widespread among major UK companies. An FCA review found that 92% of FTSE 350 companies disclosed climate risks in their 2025 annual reports.
Britain’s financial regulator has stepped back from tougher mandatory climate disclosure requirements for listed companies, citing concerns over costs, proportionality and international competitiveness.
The Financial Conduct Authority had proposed in January that listed companies adopt a new UK climate-reporting standard. The requirements would have covered financially material climate risks and opportunities, corporate climate targets and the potential impact of climate change on businesses.
Under final rules published on Wednesday, companies will instead retain greater flexibility through the existing “comply or explain” approach. Businesses can choose not to make certain disclosures if they provide an explanation.
The decision places the UK within a wider international retreat from more prescriptive corporate sustainability reporting.
Competitiveness reshapes UK disclosure policy
Feedback to the FCA questioned whether mandatory adoption of UK SRS S2 would be proportionate. The standard is the UK-endorsed version of the International Sustainability Standards Board’s climate disclosure standard.
Companies also raised concerns about implementation costs and whether stricter requirements could weaken the UK’s competitiveness as a listing destination.
The Quoted Companies Alliance, which represents UK-listed companies, welcomed regulatory measures that provide greater flexibility and proportionality.
For policymakers, the challenge is balancing those concerns against investors’ demand for consistent and comparable climate information.
Ian Bhullar, director for sustainability policy at UK Finance, said the change should reduce companies’ reporting burden. However, it could also limit information available to lenders and investors assessing sustainability risks and corporate strategies.
That trade-off is becoming increasingly prominent as governments reconsider the scope and cost of ESG regulation.
RELATED ARTICLE: FCA Sets Out Findings from Climate Reporting Review of Financial Firms
Climate reporting rules retreat across major markets
The UK decision follows regulatory changes elsewhere.
The European Union has moved to reduce parts of its corporate sustainability reporting framework. In the United States, the Trump administration has abandoned plans for federal climate-reporting rules.
These developments are changing the competitive landscape for financial centres. Regulators must now consider whether imposing tougher disclosure requirements could disadvantage domestic markets when peer jurisdictions are reducing their own requirements.
Carmen Nuzzo, executive director of the TPI Global Climate Transition Centre at the London School of Economics and Political Science, said questions remain about the durability of voluntary disclosure and the comparability of resulting data.
“Regulatory competitiveness arguments tend to gain traction when peer jurisdictions retreat first … particularly when jurisdictions compete for listing,” she said.
The concern for investors is that greater flexibility could eventually produce less consistent information across companies. That could make climate risks more difficult to compare, particularly across sectors and jurisdictions.
Existing disclosure levels remain high
The FCA’s decision does not remove climate reporting from the UK listing framework.
The regulator first introduced climate disclosure rules in 2020 for premium-listed companies. Businesses were asked to report climate-related risks in line with the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures framework, or explain why they had not done so.
Those requirements were later expanded to other categories of listed companies.
Disclosure rates have remained high. An FCA review of FTSE 350 companies’ 2025 annual reports found that 92% had disclosed climate risks.
That existing level of participation will now become an important test of the FCA’s approach. Investors will be watching whether disclosure remains widespread without a stricter mandate, and whether the quality and comparability of reporting improve.
For boards and executives, the regulatory burden may be lighter than initially proposed. Investor expectations around material climate risks, however, have not disappeared.
The UK’s decision also adds to a broader shift in global ESG governance. Regulators are increasingly weighing climate transparency against compliance costs and capital-market competitiveness. How companies respond voluntarily will help determine whether that balance can deliver decision-useful climate information without another round of mandatory rules.

articles.full_text:
Cotierra Raises $3M to Scale Biochar Across Tropical Agriculture
- $3 million raised: Cotierra will use the new capital to move its decentralised biochar technology from field deployments to repeatable commercial scale.
- $4.75 million total funding: The Zurich climate technology company has attracted investors spanning food, agriculture, carbon removal and impact investing.
- Supply-chain focus: Cotierra converts agricultural residues into biochar near farms, targeting soil resilience, farmer productivity, supply-chain emissions and durable carbon removal.
Cotierra has raised $3 million to scale its decentralised biochar technology across tropical agricultural supply chains, following successful deployments in the coffee sector.
The Zurich-based climate technology company has now raised approximately $4.75 million since its founding. The latest capital will support its transition from individual field deployments to a repeatable commercial model combining hardware, software and carbon monitoring.
The round was co-led by PINC, the venture arm of international food and beverage company Paulig, and Carbon Removal Partners. Zürcher Kantonalbank, Carbon Drawdown Initiative, better ventures, GOTA Ventures, Hungry4Impact and Triple Impact Ventures also participated. Climate and impact-focused angel investors joined the round.
Turning agricultural waste into a climate asset
Cotierra is targeting a persistent problem across tropical agricultural economies. Large volumes of residual biomass are generated across farming supply chains, yet much of this material remains unused.
At the same time, deteriorating soil health and increasingly frequent extreme weather are putting pressure on agricultural productivity. Those challenges extend beyond farmers. Food and beverage companies face growing physical climate risks across supply chains while working to reduce Scope 3 emissions.
Cotierra’s system converts agricultural residues into biochar close to where the biomass is produced. The biochar can then be returned to agricultural soils, where it stores carbon and can support soil quality and resilience.
The company’s technology combines decentralised reactors with a digital platform for operating, monitoring and verifying biochar production. This provides agricultural businesses with data to track production and environmental outcomes.
For corporate buyers, the model links carbon removal with a broader supply-chain resilience strategy rather than treating the two as separate objectives.
Coffee deployments provide commercial test case
Cotierra has already deployed its technology within the coffee value chain. The company is now developing those field-tested systems into an integrated hardware and software product that can be replicated across regions and agricultural commodities.
It said a strong order backlog is supporting its next phase of expansion.
Thomas Käslin, CEO and Co-Founder, Cotierra said: “We have shown that decentralised biochar offers a highly effective pathway to decarbonise and strengthen tropical agricultural value chains where biomass is widely dispersed. Now we are making it simple, reliable and scalable. Our ambition is to make it the standard solution for agricultural companies to strengthen farmer productivity and resilience while reducing emissions and removing carbon across their supply chains.”
The participation of Paulig’s venture arm also illustrates the commercial interest in technologies that address both agricultural resilience and corporate climate targets.
Karl Swensson, Investment Director, PINC said: “For a food and beverage company like Paulig, the long-term resilience and productivity of agricultural value chains are fundamental. What stood out to us about Cotierra is the strong traction the company has achieved with coffee traders through a solution that delivers value for farmers, traders and coffee companies alike. We believe decentralised biochar can play an important role in reducing emissions and improving resilience in coffee-growing regions. As part of a broader portfolio of climate solutions, it has significant potential to contribute to Paulig’s coffee climate ambitions.”
Carbon removal moves closer to the farm
Biochar has attracted growing interest within carbon removal because it can lock carbon into a stable form while using biomass that might otherwise have limited economic value. Cotierra’s approach adds another dimension by locating production within agricultural value chains rather than relying on centralised facilities.
RELATED ARTICLE: Mangrove Systems Expands Biochar MRV Platform With Grain Ecosystem Acquisition
Max Zeller, Founder & Partner, Carbon Removal Partners said: “Cotierra addresses a major untapped opportunity in tropical agriculture by leveraging agricultural waste to create resilient value chains, while delivering environmental benefits. Since our first investment, the team has transformed a strong technical concept into proven results in the field and gained significant commercial traction with many of the world’s largest coffee producers. Cotierra has built the foundation to become a leading technology platform for more resilient and higher-yielding value chains across the tropics.”
For food and beverage companies, the business case will depend on whether decentralised systems can deliver consistent economics, measurable carbon removal and credible verification at scale.
If Cotierra can replicate its coffee deployments across other crops and regions, the model could connect three priorities increasingly competing for corporate capital: supply security, agricultural resilience and supply-chain decarbonisation.

articles.title: EIB, BNP Paribas Back $794 Million Guarantee Plan for EU Power Grids
articles.summary:
The European Investment Bank and BNP Paribas are expanding financing support for Europe’s electricity grids as the region confronts rising demand for infrastructure needed to electrify its economy. Under a […]
The post EIB, BNP Paribas Back $794 Million Guarantee Plan for EU Power Grids appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
EIB, BNP Paribas Back $794 Million Guarantee Plan for EU Power Grids
- EIB and BNP Paribas will build a guarantee portfolio of up to $794 million to support European electricity grid component manufacturers.
- The risk-sharing structure is expected to unlock as much as $3.18 billion in real-economy investment across the European Union.
- The deal forms part of the EIB’s $1.70 billion Pan-EU Power Grid package, backed by the EU’s InvestEU programme.
The European Investment Bank and BNP Paribas are expanding financing support for Europe’s electricity grids as the region confronts rising demand for infrastructure needed to electrify its economy.
Under a new agreement, the EIB will provide up to $397 million in counter-guarantees. BNP Paribas will commit an equivalent amount. Together, the institutions will create a bank guarantee portfolio worth up to $794 million for manufacturers supplying electricity grid equipment.
The financing structure is expected to mobilise up to $3.18 billion in investment in the real economy.
The agreement targets a growing bottleneck in Europe’s energy transition. Expanding renewable generation and electrifying transport, buildings and industry require substantial investment in transmission and distribution networks. Manufacturers must also expand production of the equipment needed to build them.
Financing Europe’s grid supply chain
The risk-sharing structure will increase BNP Paribas’ capacity to provide guarantees to European manufacturers of critical grid components. These guarantees can help companies secure contracts, expand production and respond to growing orders without placing the full financing burden on their balance sheets.
For the EIB, the agreement links infrastructure investment with industrial competitiveness and energy security.
EIB Vice-President Ambroise Fayolle said: “We are pleased to continue our cooperation with BNP Paribas on Europe’s energy security and green transition. Following our agreement on wind energy last year, we have now concluded a risk-sharing agreement to support companies manufacturing the equipment essential for developing energy grids. In 2025, the EIB Group invested $37.42 billion in energy worldwide, including $13.15 billion in grids and storage. In 2026, we are continuing this commitment with the same level of ambition.”
The EIB’s 2025 figures are equivalent to approximately $37.42 billion in global energy investment, including about $13.15 billion for grids and storage.
Rodolfe Vergeaud, Co-Head of Transaction Banking, Head of Trade and Working Capital BNP Paribas CIB EMEA, said: “Strengthening Europe’s electricity grids requires mobilising all players throughout the value chain. This agreement with the EIB enables us to go further in supporting manufacturers of essential electricity grid components by increasing our capacity to meet their guarantee needs and support their development.”
RELATED ARTICLE: EIB Invests $46 Million in Modular Nuclear
EU financing shifts toward grid capacity
The agreement sits within the EIB’s $1.70 billion Pan-EU Power Grid package, which is dedicated to developing, modernising and strengthening electricity networks across the bloc. The initiative receives support from the European Union’s InvestEU programme.
It follows a broader EIB push to finance the infrastructure and manufacturing capacity behind Europe’s energy transition.
The bank previously made approximately $7.37 billion available for wind energy. BNP Paribas also participates in that initiative. The two institutions signed an agreement in February 2025 covering a guarantee portfolio equivalent to about $1.13 billion.
The latest transaction shifts attention further into the grid infrastructure needed to connect new generation capacity and manage changing electricity flows.
Grid investment becomes an industrial priority
For investors and corporate leaders, Europe’s grid expansion is increasingly both an infrastructure challenge and a supply-chain issue.
Capital for renewable generation alone cannot deliver Europe’s energy transition if grid connections, transmission capacity and equipment manufacturing fail to keep pace. Financing mechanisms that reduce risk for suppliers can therefore influence how quickly planned infrastructure moves from development into construction.
The EIB and BNP Paribas structure also shows how public guarantees can be used to draw commercial banking capacity into strategic sectors without relying solely on direct public investment.
For the European Union, that financing model serves several priorities at once. It supports electrification, strengthens domestic manufacturing capacity and reduces infrastructure constraints that could slow renewable deployment.
As electricity demand grows and Europe pursues greater energy security, the ability to finance the companies building the grid itself is becoming central to the region’s climate and industrial strategy.

articles.title: Google Invests $1.2 Million in Chile Water Resilience Project
articles.summary:
Google is investing $1.2 million in a water infrastructure project designed to reduce losses from an irrigation canal in Chile’s Maipo River Basin. The funding will support Aguas Andinas in […]

articles.full_text:
Google Invests $1.2 Million in Chile Water Resilience Project
- Google is contributing $1.2 million to improve irrigation infrastructure in Chile’s Maipo River Basin, a critical water source for Santiago.
- The project could save up to 7.4 million cubic meters of water each year by reducing seepage from a major irrigation canal.
- The investment forms part of Google’s wider water stewardship strategy as data center operators face growing scrutiny over water consumption and local resource pressures.
Google is investing $1.2 million in a water infrastructure project designed to reduce losses from an irrigation canal in Chile’s Maipo River Basin.
The funding will support Aguas Andinas in lining a 2.5-kilometer section of the Unidos de Buin Canal Association’s main irrigation canal. The project aims to conserve water used by local agriculture while improving the health of the surrounding watershed.
Google operates a data center in Quilicura, within the Santiago metropolitan region. The company said its water stewardship efforts replenished more water to the Maipo River Basin in 2025 than its Quilicura facility consumed.
Cutting water losses in a critical watershed
The Maipo River Basin is a vital source of water for Santiago and surrounding agricultural areas. Improving water efficiency within the basin has become increasingly important as competing demands place pressure on available supplies.
Google’s investment will finance concrete lining along part of the existing irrigation canal. The upgrade is intended to prevent water from escaping through seepage before reaching agricultural users.
Over its lifespan, the project is estimated to conserve up to 7.4 million cubic meters of water annually. That is equivalent to approximately 1.9 billion gallons.
The infrastructure work is also expected to reduce sedimentation and erosion. This could improve water quality while helping the canal operate more efficiently.
For agricultural communities, the project is focused on retaining a greater share of existing water supplies rather than developing new sources. That distinction matters in regions where water availability is increasingly contested among cities, industry, agriculture and ecosystems.
Data center growth puts water use in focus
The investment comes as the rapid expansion of data centers increases attention on the sector’s environmental footprint. Artificial intelligence and cloud computing require large amounts of computing capacity, creating additional demand for both electricity and cooling.
Data centers generate significant heat during operation. Operators can use water-based cooling systems to reduce energy requirements, but that approach creates trade-offs between water and electricity consumption.
RELATED ARTICLE: Google Backs Near-Zero Emissions Steel Plant
Google says it takes a climate-conscious approach to cooling its facilities and balances those competing resource demands.
Its Chile project also reflects a broader shift in corporate water strategies. Companies with water-intensive operations are increasingly looking beyond efficiency measures inside their own facilities. Watershed restoration, replenishment and shared infrastructure projects can address risks across the wider systems on which businesses and communities depend.
Google has committed to replenishing more water than it consumes and improving watershed health in communities where it operates. Its stewardship program includes investments developed with local organizations to address specific watershed challenges.
Water risk moves further up the ESG agenda
For companies expanding digital infrastructure, water availability is becoming a material site-selection and operational consideration alongside electricity supply, grid capacity and carbon intensity.
That has implications for investors and corporate executives assessing data center growth. Water stress can create physical risks, increase operating costs and expose companies to regulatory or community opposition, particularly where industrial demand competes with household or agricultural needs.
Local infrastructure investments can help address those pressures, but governance remains central. Companies must demonstrate how projects affect water availability across entire watersheds and whether claimed replenishment translates into durable benefits for local users.
In Chile, Google’s funding connects the water footprint of digital infrastructure with an established agricultural system serving the Maipo basin.
As global demand for computing capacity continues to rise, projects such as the canal upgrade illustrate how water management is becoming part of the infrastructure equation. For technology companies, managing growth increasingly means accounting for the condition of the watersheds surrounding their facilities, not only the resources consumed within them.

The European Investment Bank is providing $113 million to finance Dama Solar, a 1.3 GWp solar development set to become one of Europe’s largest photovoltaic plants.
Rezolv Energy is developing the $822 million project in western Romania. Once operational, Dama Solar could generate enough electricity each year to supply more than 280,000 households, equivalent to close to one million people.
The plant will connect directly to Romania’s high-voltage electricity network. Its scale will add substantial renewable generation capacity to the national grid as Romania seeks to strengthen domestic energy supply and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
“Europe needs more clean energy, and it needs it at scale. Dama Solar will add a major new source of renewable electricity to Romania’s energy system while bringing investment and jobs to the region,” said EIB Vice-President Ioannis Tsakiris. “It is a good example of how European investment can support energy security, climate action and regional development together.”
European capital targets energy security
The EIB financing forms part of a broader funding package for the project and is supported by InvestEU. For Romania, the investment combines energy security objectives with the EU’s push to accelerate renewable deployment and direct capital towards less-developed regions.
Dama Solar sits in Arad County, one of Romania’s cohesion regions. The project could employ around 1,500 people at peak construction over the next three years. In addition, construction and supply-chain activity should support the wider regional economy.
“We are extremely pleased to reach the financing milestone on this landmark project. The EIB team have done a fantastic job working with our other relationship lenders to deliver this transaction on an extremely aggressive timetable. EIB’s anchor ticket supported by Invest EU has played a crucial role in underpinning the wider financing package,” said, Head of Financing at Rezolv Energy Jan Viton.
The financing structure also illustrates the role of public-sector lenders in mobilising capital for utility-scale renewable infrastructure. Large projects increasingly require a mix of institutional financing and long-term revenue arrangements to manage development and power-price risk.

Long-term contracts support revenue certainty
Dama Solar has secured two 15-year Contracts for Difference covering 520 MW of its planned capacity.
Rezolv Energy plans to sell the remaining electricity into the market and supply commercial and industrial customers through long-term agreements. As a result, the project can diversify its revenue sources while giving businesses greater access to renewable electricity.
For corporate energy buyers, large developments such as Dama Solar can expand the pool of renewable generation available for long-term procurement. This is particularly relevant for companies seeking to reduce Scope 2 emissions and manage exposure to energy-price volatility.
Solar development paired with nature restoration
The project also includes an 82-hectare area dedicated to nature restoration.
Lower-quality agricultural land will be returned to pasture, while sheep will be used to manage vegetation. The restoration programme is intended to rehabilitate degraded steppe grassland and create habitat for wildlife and protected bird species.
The approach places biodiversity alongside energy generation within the project’s environmental strategy, an increasingly important consideration for investors assessing the wider impacts of renewable infrastructure.
For Romania, Dama Solar brings together several policy priorities: additional domestic generation, lower-carbon electricity, regional investment and employment.
At 1.3 GWp, its scale also makes the project relevant beyond the Romanian market. Europe’s energy transition will require substantial additions of renewable capacity alongside grid investment and long-term financing. Dama Solar shows how EU-backed capital, private development and contracted revenues can be combined to bring projects of that scale into the European power system.

Amazon, Constellation Sign 20-Year Nuclear Deal to Add 190 MW in Maryland
- Amazon has signed a 20-year power agreement with Constellation covering 690 MW from Maryland’s Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant, including 190 MW of new capacity.
- The agreement will support more than $3 billion in infrastructure investment and help fund improvements across the 1,790 MW facility.
- The additional emissions-free generation is expected between 2030 and 2032, as rising electricity demand increases pressure for reliable clean power across the PJM grid.
Amazon and Constellation have agreed a 20-year power purchase agreement that will support an expansion of Maryland’s only nuclear power plant. The deal is expected to unlock more than $3 billion in infrastructure investment and add about 190 MW of emissions-free generation.
The agreement covers 690 MW of power from the Calvert Cliffs Clean Energy Center, including the planned 190 MW capacity uprate. The additional generation is scheduled to come online between 2030 and 2032.
Amazon and Constellation have also entered a related retail supply agreement supporting Amazon operations across the 13-state PJM electricity market.
For Amazon, the arrangement provides a long-term source of carbon-free electricity while helping manage energy costs across its regional facilities. For Constellation, the contract provides revenue certainty for investment in one of Maryland’s most important electricity assets.
Extending the life of Calvert Cliffs
Calvert Cliffs has 1,790 MW of existing capacity and produces approximately 80% of Maryland’s clean energy. Its annual electricity generation is equivalent to the power needs of more than 1.3 million homes.
Amazon’s commitment will help Constellation pursue another 20-year operating license for the plant. The company also plans upgrades across the facility and is considering additional clean energy development at the site.
“This agreement demonstrates how private investment can strengthen critical energy infrastructure,” said Joe Dominguez, chairman, president and chief executive officer, Constellation. “Amazon’s commitment supports the long-term operation of Calvert Cliffs for generations to come and creates a strong foundation for future investment in both the facility and in advanced nuclear technologies.”
The agreement does not redirect Calvert Cliffs’ electricity exclusively to Amazon facilities. Power generated by the plant will continue flowing into the PJM regional grid.
That structure allows a large corporate buyer to provide financial support for new generation while keeping the resulting electricity available to the wider power system.

Data center demand reshapes clean energy procurement
The deal comes as technology companies seek increasingly large volumes of dependable electricity for data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Nuclear generation offers a combination that is difficult to replicate at scale: around-the-clock electricity without the direct carbon emissions associated with fossil fuel generation. Long-term corporate contracts can also give nuclear operators greater certainty when considering costly plant upgrades and license extensions.
“Amazon is committed to investing in carbon-free energy to strengthen the grid and benefit the communities where we operate,” said Kerry Person, vice president of AWS Global Operations and Data Center Delivery. “This long-term agreement with Constellation sustains the continued operation and expansion of Maryland’s largest source of carbon-free energy, supports hundreds of jobs, and brings significant new generation to the regional grid.”
Calvert Cliffs currently employs more than 800 people. The facility also contributes about $21 million annually in taxes that support schools, roads and other public services.
Corporate procurement moves deeper into infrastructure
For executives and investors, the agreement illustrates how corporate clean energy procurement is expanding beyond conventional renewable PPAs.
Large electricity users are increasingly entering longer-term arrangements tied to existing nuclear assets, capacity expansions and other firm power resources. Such contracts can provide developers and operators with revenue visibility while helping corporate buyers address energy availability and carbon objectives.
The Calvert Cliffs agreement also links corporate energy strategy directly with regional grid investment. Amazon gains greater long-term cost visibility, while Constellation receives support for plant upgrades, relicensing and additional capacity.
With electricity demand rising across major US data center markets, the financing of reliable clean generation is becoming a central infrastructure issue. The Maryland agreement places nuclear power firmly within that equation, connecting corporate procurement, grid reliability and long-term decarbonization investment.
